### Combining Data from Group Members

My group members and I have compiled data from all the years into similar formats. Now I will take them and stitch them together as best as possible. Below are a list of the years and who cleaned them:

 - **Mai:** 2006 & 2007 (these two years are in one large file together), 2016, 2023
 
 - **Mei:** 2019, 2020, 2024
 
 - **Nick:** 2017, 2018, 2025 (2025 had no metadata & was highly ambiguous, so it was not included in the master file.)
 
 - **Kat:** 2004, 2005, 2008 (only one sampling day recorded), 2026

**AI Statement:** AI (Claude Sonnet 5.5 Medium) was used to assist in writing code for merging these data sheets. No sensitive information from these data sheets were uploaded to AI, only the column names and specific columns isolated from the main document (such as the place names and organism names) for cleaning and standardizing purposes only.

```{r}

library(readxl)
```

### Reformatting from Wide to Long

OK- some of these are wide, and some of these are long. Let's make them all long:

```{r}

# datasets that are wide: data_17, data_18, data_19_20_24

data_17 |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(acanthophora_spicifera:zoanthid_sp),
               names_to = "organism",
               values_to = "count",
               values_drop_na = TRUE) -> data_17_long

data_18 |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(acanthophora_spicifera:valonia_sp),
               names_to = "organism",
               values_to = "count",
               values_drop_na = TRUE) -> data_18_long


data_19_20_24 |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = c(acanthophora_spicifera:unknown, unknown_bulbous_algae, actinopyga_varians:zoanthid_spp, hermit_crab),
               names_to = "organism",
               values_to = "count",
               values_drop_na = TRUE) |> 
  filter_out(count == 0) -> data_19_20_24_long



```

**Claude:**

I've written `join_dfs.R`, the data frame version of the join script. Replace `df1` through `df6` in the `dfs` list with the names of your own data frames, which need to already be loaded in your R session. It needs the `dplyr`, `purrr`, and `readr` packages.

It joins them one at a time, matching each time on every column name that the data joined so far shares with the next data frame. A message prints which columns were used for each join. It stops with an error if two tables have no shared columns, rather than silently matching on nothing.

Unlike the CSV version, this one doesn't read everything as text first, so if a shared column has different types across data frames (say numeric in one and character in another), `full_join()` will throw a type error. If that happens, convert that column to the same type in each data frame before running the script, for example with `mutate(year = as.character(year))`.

If your data frames share specific key columns, such as an ID and a year, tell me which ones and I'll set `by` explicitly, which is safer than matching on everything.

That gave an error so I copy-pasted it into Claude, which gave me this:

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## AI Chat Log - Error Troubleshooting

**Kat:**

Error in `full_join()`:
! Can't join `x$start_time` with `y$start_time` due to incompatible types.
ℹ `x$start_time` is a <character>.
ℹ `y$start_time` is a <time>.

**Claude:**

That error means `start_time` is stored as text in one data frame and as a time in another, and `full_join()` won't match across types. I've updated `join_dfs.R` to fix it.

The script now converts every column in every data frame to character before joining. After the join, `type_convert()` guesses the types again, so `start_time` should come back as a time and numbers as numbers.

Since everything is compared as text, values must be formatted identically to match. For example, `"08:30:00"` in one data frame and `"8:30"` in another won't line up. If you see more rows than expected in the result, check the formatting of your shared columns first.

Also, if any of your columns are date-times (POSIXct), converting them to character can drop the time portion for values at exactly midnight. If you have columns like that, let me know and I'll handle them separately.

:::


```{r}

# Full join six data frames on all columns they share,
# then save the result to "allyears_joined_data.csv"

# install.packages(c("dplyr", "purrr", "readr"))  # run once if needed
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(readr)

# 1. Put your six data frames in a list (edit these names) -----------------
# They must already be loaded in your R session.
dfs <- list(data_17_long, data_18_long, data_19_20_24_long, data_26, data_06_07_16_23, data_04_05_08)

# 2. Convert every column to character ---------------------------------------
# This avoids "incompatible types" errors when the same column is stored
# differently in different data frames (e.g. character vs. time).
# Types are restored in step 4.
dfs <- map(dfs, ~ mutate(.x, across(everything(), as.character)))

# 3. Full join, one data frame at a time -----------------------------------
# Each join matches on every column name that the data joined so far
# shares with the next data frame (a "natural" join).
joined <- reduce(dfs, function(x, y) {
  shared <- intersect(names(x), names(y))
  if (length(shared) == 0) {
    stop("No shared columns found between the data joined so far and the next data frame.")
  }
  message("Joining on: ", paste(shared, collapse = ", "))
  full_join(x, y, by = shared)
})

# 4. Restore sensible column types -----------------------------------------
joined <- type_convert(joined)

# 5. Write the result ------------------------------------------------------
write_csv(joined, here("Kat", "OPIHI_Project", "Data", "mai_mei_nick_kat_combined_years", "allyears_joined_data.csv"))

message("Saved ", nrow(joined), " rows and ", ncol(joined),
        " columns to allyears_joined_data.csv")


```

## AI Chat Log - Removing Prefixes in Column Names

**Kat:**

write me a script in R that removes the string "meta_" from every column name in a dataframe, then merges any columns that now have the same name.

**Claude:**

I've written `remove_meta_merge.R`. Replace `df` with the name of your data frame. The merged result is saved as `df_merged`, and your original `df` is left unchanged only if you rename it in step 1, since the script reassigns `df` as it goes. The script needs the `dplyr` package.

It strips `"meta_"` from every column name, wherever it appears in the name. For example, `meta_id` and `id` both become `id`. Columns that now share a name are combined into one by taking the first non-missing value in each row, going left to right. Column order follows the first appearance of each name.

If two same-named columns both have a value in the same row and the values differ, the leftmost column wins. If your columns can conflict like that, check them before merging. If the duplicate columns have different types (for example, one numeric and one character), they're compared as text, so the merged column ends up as character.

If you only want to remove `"meta_"` when it's at the start of the name, change the `gsub()` line to `gsub("^meta_", "", names(df))`.

:::



```{r}
#| collapse: true

# Remove "meta_" from every column name, then merge columns that now share a name

# install.packages("dplyr")  # run once if needed
library(dplyr)

# 1. Start from your data frame (edit the name) ----------------------------
# as.data.frame() makes sure duplicate column names are allowed in step 2.
df <- as.data.frame(all_joined)

# 2. Remove "meta_" from every column name ---------------------------------
names(df) <- gsub("meta_", "", names(df), fixed = TRUE)

# 3. Merge columns that now have the same name -----------------------------
# For each set of same-named columns, take the first non-missing value
# in each row (left to right).
new_names <- unique(names(df))

merged <- lapply(new_names, function(nm) {
  cols <- unname(as.list(df[, names(df) == nm, drop = FALSE]))

  # If the duplicate columns have different types, compare them as text
  types <- vapply(cols, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1))
  if (length(unique(types)) > 1) cols <- lapply(cols, as.character)

  Reduce(coalesce, cols)
})
names(merged) <- new_names

all_joined_merged <- as.data.frame(merged, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# 4. Check the result ------------------------------------------------------
message(ncol(df), " columns reduced to ", ncol(all_joined_merged))
print(names(all_joined_merged))

# Optional: save to disk
# write.csv(df_merged, "df_merged.csv", row.names = FALSE)

```

## AI Chat Log - More Prefix Removal

**Kat:**

Great! Write me a script in R that does the same exact thing, but with the string "x_"

**Claude:**

I've written `remove_x_merge.R`. It works the same way as the `meta_` version: replace `df` in step 1 with the name of your data frame, and the merged result is saved as `df_merged`. This version also works on a copy (`df_work`), so your original data frame isn't changed.

`"x_"` is a much shorter string than `"meta_"`, so it's more likely to appear inside other column names. For example, `max_value` would become `mavalue`, and `index_id` would become `indeid`. If you only want to strip it from the start of a name (like `x_id` becoming `id`), use the commented-out `gsub("^x_", ...)` line in step 2 in place of the one below it.

```{r}
#| collapse: true

# Remove "x_" from every column name, then merge columns that now share a name

# install.packages("dplyr")  # run once if needed

# 1. Make a working copy of your data frame (edit the name) ----------------
# as.data.frame() makes sure duplicate column names are allowed in step 2.
df_work <- as.data.frame(all_joined_merged)

# 2. Remove "x_" from every column name ------------------------------------
# Note: this removes "x_" anywhere in a name, so "max_value" would become
# "mavalue". To remove it only at the start of a name, use this instead:
# names(df_work) <- gsub("^x_", "", names(df_work))
names(df_work) <- gsub("x_", "", names(df_work), fixed = TRUE)

# 3. Merge columns that now have the same name -----------------------------
# For each set of same-named columns, take the first non-missing value
# in each row (left to right).
new_names <- unique(names(df_work))

merged <- lapply(new_names, function(nm) {
  cols <- unname(as.list(df_work[, names(df_work) == nm, drop = FALSE]))

  # If the duplicate columns have different types, compare them as text
  types <- vapply(cols, function(x) class(x)[1], character(1))
  if (length(unique(types)) > 1) cols <- lapply(cols, as.character)

  Reduce(coalesce, cols)
})
names(merged) <- new_names

final_df_merged <- as.data.frame(merged, check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# 4. Check the result ------------------------------------------------------
message(ncol(df_work), " columns reduced to ", ncol(final_df_merged))
print(names(final_df_merged))

# Optional: save to disk
# write.csv(df_merged, "df_merged.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

But I do not want anything that is overlapping in data. If it overlaps, I do not want to combine the data, as it means they are likely two different measurements instead of the same with different column names.


::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## AI Chat Log - Joining Columns Function (Without Overlap!)

**Kat:**

Write me an R script that will join two specific columns in a dataframe if, after dropping NAs, the two columns do not overlap in data.

**Claude:**

This script checks whether the two columns overlap, and only merges them if they don't. I've read "overlap" as **the two columns never both have a value in the same row** (after ignoring `NA`s), since that's the case where merging loses nothing. If you meant something different, see the note below the code.

```r
merge_if_no_overlap <- function(df, col1, col2, new_col = "merged",
                                drop_originals = TRUE) {
  a <- df[[col1]]
  b <- df[[col2]]

  # Overlap = any row where both columns have a non-NA value
  overlap_rows <- which(!is.na(a) & !is.na(b))

  if (length(overlap_rows) > 0) {
    warning(sprintf(
      "Columns '%s' and '%s' overlap in %d row(s) (e.g., row %d). No merge performed.",
      col1, col2, length(overlap_rows), overlap_rows[1]
    ))
    return(df)
  }

  # No overlap: take whichever value is present (keeps the original data type)
  merged <- a
  merged[is.na(a)] <- b[is.na(a)]

  df[[new_col]] <- merged
  if (drop_originals) {
    df[, c(col1, col2)] <- NULL
  }
  df
}

# --- Example 1: no overlap -> merges ---
df_ok <- data.frame(
  id   = 1:4,
  col1 = c("A", NA, "C", NA),
  col2 = c(NA, "B", NA, NA),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
result_ok <- merge_if_no_overlap(df_ok, "col1", "col2", new_col = "merged")
print(result_ok)

# --- Example 2: overlap in row 1 -> warns and leaves df unchanged ---
df_bad <- data.frame(
  id   = 1:3,
  col1 = c("A", NA, "C"),
  col2 = c("X", "B", NA),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
result_bad <- merge_if_no_overlap(df_bad, "col1", "col2")
print(result_bad)
```

**How it works:**

- **Overlap check:** `!is.na(a) & !is.na(b)` flags rows where both columns hold data. If any exist, the function warns you (with the count and first offending row) and returns the data frame untouched.
- **Merge:** when there's no overlap, each row has at most one value, so filling the `NA`s in `col1` from `col2` gives the combined column. Rows where both are `NA` stay `NA`.
- **Options:** `new_col` sets the name of the result, and `drop_originals = FALSE` keeps the original two columns.

**If you meant a different kind of overlap:** some people mean the two columns share the same *values* anywhere (e.g., "A" appears in both, in any rows), not just in the same row. To check that instead, replace the overlap test with:

```r
shared_values <- intersect(na.omit(a), na.omit(b))
if (length(shared_values) > 0) { ... }
```

And if both columns can have values in the same row under that definition, you'd join them as text (like the `paste()` approach from before) rather than filling gaps. Let me know which you need and I can adjust it.


:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## AI Chat Log - Rephrasing

**Kat:**

Write me an R script that will join two specific columns in a dataframe if, after dropping NAs, the two columns do not overlap in data. If the two columns contain the exact same data, merge them anyway.

**Claude:**

This version merges the columns when there's no overlap, or when they contain exactly the same data. Otherwise it warns and returns the data frame unchanged.

```r
merge_if_compatible <- function(df, col1, col2, new_col = "merged",
                                drop_originals = TRUE,
                                allow_agreeing_overlap = FALSE) {
  a <- df[[col1]]
  b <- df[[col2]]

  # Avoid factor comparison problems
  if (is.factor(a)) a <- as.character(a)
  if (is.factor(b)) b <- as.character(b)

  # Rows where both columns have a value
  both <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)

  # Case 1: no overlap (no row has a value in both columns)
  no_overlap <- !any(both)

  # Case 2: exact same data (same NA positions and same values everywhere)
  exact_same <- identical(is.na(a), is.na(b)) &&
    all(a[!is.na(a)] == b[!is.na(b)])

  # Optional relaxed rule: overlapping rows are allowed if the values agree
  agreeing_overlap <- allow_agreeing_overlap && all(a[both] == b[both])

  if (!(no_overlap || exact_same || agreeing_overlap)) {
    warning(sprintf(
      "Columns '%s' and '%s' overlap with different values in %d row(s) (e.g., row %d). No merge performed.",
      col1, col2, sum(both & a != b), which(both & a != b)[1]
    ))
    return(df)
  }

  # Merge: take col1, fill its NAs from col2
  merged <- a
  merged[is.na(a)] <- b[is.na(a)]

  df[[new_col]] <- merged
  if (drop_originals) df[, c(col1, col2)] <- NULL
  df
}

# --- Example 1: no overlap -> merges ---
df1 <- data.frame(id = 1:4,
                  col1 = c("A", NA, "C", NA),
                  col2 = c(NA, "B", NA, NA))
df1 |> merge_if_compatible("col1", "col2") |> print()

# --- Example 2: identical columns -> merges anyway ---
df2 <- data.frame(id = 1:3,
                  col1 = c("A", "B", NA),
                  col2 = c("A", "B", NA))
df2 |> merge_if_compatible("col1", "col2") |> print()

# --- Example 3: conflicting overlap -> warns, df unchanged ---
df3 <- data.frame(id = 1:3,
                  col1 = c("A", NA, "C"),
                  col2 = c("X", "B", NA))
df3 |> merge_if_compatible("col1", "col2") |> print()
```

**How the rules work:**

- **No overlap:** no row has a value in both columns, so merging loses nothing.
- **Exact same data:** the columns have `NA`s in the same rows and equal values everywhere else. This is the case the overlap check alone would reject, which is why it gets its own test.
- **Anything else** (a row where both columns have different values) triggers the warning and leaves the data frame untouched.

**Optional relaxed rule:** by default, "exact same" means the whole columns match, including where the `NA`s fall. If you'd rather merge whenever the rows that overlap agree with each other, even if one column has extra values the other lacks, use `allow_agreeing_overlap = TRUE`:

```r
df |> merge_if_compatible("col1", "col2", allow_agreeing_overlap = TRUE)
```

**Notes:**

- Factor columns are converted to character before merging, so the merged column is text.
- Use `drop_originals = FALSE` to keep the original two columns, and `new_col` to name the result.
- Values are compared with `==`, so `"a"` and `"A"` count as different.


:::


```{r}

merge_if_compatible <- function(df, col1, col2, new_col = "merged",
                                drop_originals = TRUE,
                                allow_agreeing_overlap = FALSE) {
  a <- df[[col1]]
  b <- df[[col2]]

  # Avoid factor comparison problems
  if (is.factor(a)) a <- as.character(a)
  if (is.factor(b)) b <- as.character(b)

  # Rows where both columns have a value
  both <- !is.na(a) & !is.na(b)

  # Case 1: no overlap (no row has a value in both columns)
  no_overlap <- !any(both)

  # Case 2: exact same data (same NA positions and same values everywhere)
  exact_same <- identical(is.na(a), is.na(b)) &&
    all(a[!is.na(a)] == b[!is.na(b)])

  # Optional relaxed rule: overlapping rows are allowed if the values agree
  agreeing_overlap <- allow_agreeing_overlap && all(a[both] == b[both])

  if (!(no_overlap || exact_same || agreeing_overlap)) {
    warning(sprintf(
      "Columns '%s' and '%s' overlap with different values in %d row(s) (e.g., row %d). No merge performed.",
      col1, col2, sum(both & a != b), which(both & a != b)[1]
    ))
    return(df)
  }

  # Merge: take col1, fill its NAs from col2
  merged <- a
  merged[is.na(a)] <- b[is.na(a)]

  df[[new_col]] <- merged
  if (drop_originals) df[, c(col1, col2)] <- NULL
  df
}

# using the new function, merge school names:

final_df_merged <- merge_if_compatible(final_df_merged, "number_of_transect_lines", "n_transect_lines", new_col = "total_transect_n", allow_agreeing_overlap = TRUE)



```

## AI Chat Log - Fixing/Removing Units in Column

**Kat:**

I have a column with the following unique entries: "1 meter", "2 meters", "1/2 meter", "3 meters", "5 meters", "1.5 meters", "4 meters", "1/4 meter", "2.5 meters". Write me an R script that will remove the " meter" and " meters" part of each entry, and convert any fractions to decimals. Do not keep the original column.

**Claude:**

```r
library(dplyr)

# Converts entries like "1/2 meter" or "2.5 meters" to numeric values
clean_meters <- function(x) {
  x <- x |>
    as.character() |>
    sub(pattern = "\\s*meters?\\s*$", replacement = "", ignore.case = TRUE) |>
    trimws()

  vapply(x, function(s) {
    if (is.na(s) || s == "") return(NA_real_)
    if (grepl("/", s, fixed = TRUE)) {
      parts <- as.numeric(strsplit(s, "/", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])
      parts[1] / parts[2]
    } else {
      as.numeric(s)
    }
  }, numeric(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}

# Apply it, overwriting the original column (replace `point_spacing` with your column name)
df <- df |>
  mutate(point_spacing = clean_meters(point_spacing))

# Quick test with your unique entries
test <- c("1 meter", "2 meters", "1/2 meter", "3 meters", "5 meters",
          "1.5 meters", "4 meters", "1/4 meter", "2.5 meters")
clean_meters(test)
#> [1] 1.0 2.0 0.5 3.0 5.0 1.5 4.0 0.25 2.5
```

- **Original column:** `mutate()` assigns the result back to the same column name, so the original text version is replaced, not kept.
- **Result type:** the column becomes numeric, so you can do math on it. The unit (meters) is now implied, so you may want to rename the column to something like `point_spacing_m`.
- **Fractions:** anything with a `/` is split and divided, so `"1/2"` becomes `0.5` and `"1/4"` becomes `0.25`.
- **Other entries:** `NA`s stay `NA`. Entries the function can't parse come back as `NA` with a warning, so you'll know if an unexpected value slips in. Mixed numbers like `"1 1/2 meters"` aren't handled, since none appear in your list.

If you'd rather use base R without `dplyr`, replace the `mutate()` call with `df$point_spacing <- clean_meters(df$point_spacing)`.

:::


```{r}


# Converts entries like "1/2 meter" or "2.5 meters" to numeric values
clean_meters <- function(x) {
  x <- x |>
    as.character() |>
    sub(pattern = "\\s*meters?\\s*$", replacement = "", ignore.case = TRUE) |>
    trimws()

  vapply(x, function(s) {
    if (is.na(s) || s == "") return(NA_real_)
    if (grepl("/", s, fixed = TRUE)) {
      parts <- as.numeric(strsplit(s, "/", fixed = TRUE)[[1]])
      parts[1] / parts[2]
    } else {
      as.numeric(s)
    }
  }, numeric(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}

# Apply it, overwriting the original column (replace `point_spacing` with your column name)
final_df_merged <- final_df_merged |>
  mutate(point_spacing = clean_meters(point_spacing))

```

Your CSV has two formats, plus `NA`:
- `T-1 Q-2 at point 4.00`
- `transect-2 quadrat-1 at point 0.00`
- `NA` stays `NA` in all three new columns

The pattern ignores case and accepts `T` or `transect` and `Q` or `quadrat`. It also tolerates `-`, `_`, or a space between a label and its number, and it makes "at" optional. That should cover most other variants you might run into. Point values can be negative or decimal, so `-1.00`, `8.50`, and `4.25` all parse correctly. `transect` and `quadrat` come out as integers, and `point` as numeric.

If a non-missing entry doesn't match the pattern, it gets `NA` in the new columns and the function prints a warning listing those values, so nothing is silently lost.

R isn't available in my environment, so I couldn't run the script itself. I tested the same regular expression in Python against all 472 non-NA entries in your CSV, and every one matched, including the negative point value. The script uses base R only, so no packages need installing. If you hit any trouble, send me the output and I'll fix it.

If your column has a different name, pass it as the second argument: `separate_quadrat_sample(df, "other_name")`.

:::



```{r}
#| collapse: true

#' Split a "quadrat_sample" column into transect, quadrat, and point columns
#'
#' Handles entries such as:
#'   "T-1 Q-2 at point 4.00"
#'   "transect-2 quadrat-1 at point 0.00"
#'   NA (left as NA in all three new columns)
#'
#' The pattern is deliberately flexible: it is case-insensitive, accepts
#' "T" or "transect" and "Q" or "quadrat", tolerates "-", "_", or a space
#' (or nothing) between the label and its number, makes "at" optional, and
#' allows negative or decimal point values (e.g. "-1.00", "8.50").
#'
#' Base R only; no packages needed.

separate_quadrat_sample <- function(df, col = "quadrat_sample") {

  if (!col %in% names(df)) {
    stop("Column '", col, "' not found in the dataframe.")
  }

  x <- trimws(as.character(df[[col]]))

  pattern <- paste0(
    "^(?:transect|t)\\s*[-_ ]?\\s*(\\d+)\\s+",       # transect number
    "(?:quadrat|q)\\s*[-_ ]?\\s*(\\d+)\\s+",         # quadrat number
    "(?:at\\s+)?point\\s*(-?\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)$"  # point value
  )

  # Capture groups for every entry (NA where there is no match)
  m <- regmatches(x, regexec(pattern, x, ignore.case = TRUE, perl = TRUE))

  pull_group <- function(i) {
    vapply(m, function(z) if (length(z) == 4) z[i + 1] else NA_character_,
           character(1))
  }

  df$transect_col <- as.integer(pull_group(1))
  df$quadrat_col  <- as.integer(pull_group(2))
  df$point_col    <- as.numeric(pull_group(3))

  # Report anything that was non-missing but didn't match the pattern
  unmatched <- !is.na(x) & x != "" & is.na(df$transect_col)
  if (any(unmatched)) {
    warning(
      sum(unmatched), " row(s) in '", col, "' did not match the expected ",
      "format and were set to NA. Unmatched values:\n  ",
      paste(unique(x[unmatched]), collapse = "\n  ")
    )
  }

  df
}

# ---- Example usage ---------------------------------------------------------
# df <- read.csv("your_data.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# df <- separate_quadrat_sample(df)              # uses "quadrat_sample"
# df <- separate_quadrat_sample(df, "other_col") # or specify another name
#
# Quick test with the formats in your file:
# test <- data.frame(quadrat_sample = c("T-1 Q-1 at point 0.00",
#                                       "transect-2 quadrat-4 at point 3.00",
#                                       "T-5 Q-1 at point -1.00",
#                                       "T-5 Q-3 at point 8.50",
#                                       NA))
# separate_quadrat_sample(test)


# run the new function

  select(!quadrat_sample) -> final_df_toclean

# Look at the column names
```

Columns missing from your dataframe are skipped, and any column not on my list goes at the end, so nothing gets dropped. The function also prints a message listing both cases.

I couldn't run R here, so this is untested, but it only uses basic indexing.

You now have both `transect_number` and `transect_col`, and both `quadrat` and `quadrat_col`. I put each pair next to each other. If they hold the same information, you may want to drop one of each. You can also change the order by editing the `col_order` vector at the top of the function.

:::


```{r}


#' Reorder dataframe columns into logical groups:
#'   when/where -> who -> conditions -> transect design -> sample location -> observations
#'
#' Base R only. Columns missing from the dataframe are skipped silently, and
#' any columns not listed here are kept and placed at the end (so nothing is
#' ever dropped).

reorder_columns <- function(df) {

  col_order <- c(
    # --- When and where ---------------------------------------------------
    "date", "year", "start_time", "stop_time",
    "site_name", "latitude", "longitude",

    # --- Who --------------------------------------------------------------
    "name_of_school", "in_field_group", "group", "team_members",
    "team_lead_or_recorder", "data_entry_by",

    # --- Site conditions and activity -------------------------------------
    "low_tide_time", "low_tide_height",
    "weather", "rain_events", "wave_height", "wind_speed",
    "stressful_events", "visitors", "fishing", "collecting", "what_collecting",

    # --- Transect / survey design -----------------------------------------
    "method",
    "total_number_of_transect_lines", "length_of_transect_line", "longest_t_m",
    "total_number_of_transect_points", "dist_between_t_pts_for_q",
    "quad_t", "n_quadrats_per_transect", "point_spacing",

    # --- Location of each sample (transect > quadrat > point) -------------
    "transect_number", "transect_col",
    "quadrat", "quadrat_col", "quadrat_location_m", "quadrat_total_points",
    "point_col", "p1_or_p2", "position_on_transect_m",

    # --- Observations -----------------------------------------------------
    "organism_or_substrate_type", "category", "count",
    "within_2m_proximity_of_attached_coral_colony_y_n_mamala_bay_only",
    "sediment_depth", "notes"
  )

  present <- col_order[col_order %in% names(df)]
  extras  <- setdiff(names(df), present)

  missing <- setdiff(col_order, names(df))
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    message("Not found in dataframe (skipped): ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
  }
  if (length(extras) > 0) {
    message("Not in the order list (placed at end): ", paste(extras, collapse = ", "))
  }

  df[, c(present, extras), drop = FALSE]
}

# ---- Example usage ---------------------------------------------------------
# df <- reorder_columns(df)
#
# With dplyr you could instead write:
#   df <- dplyr::select(df, dplyr::any_of(col_order), dplyr::everything())

# reorder with the function
final_df_toclean |>
  reorder_columns() -> reordered_data


# merge the new columns with the existing columns containing the same values
reordered_data |> 
  merge_if_compatible("transect_number", "transect_col", new_col = "transect_id", allow_agreeing_overlap = TRUE) |>
  merge_if_compatible("quadrat", "quadrat_col", new_col = "quadrat_id", allow_agreeing_overlap = TRUE) |> 
  merge_if_compatible("point_col", "position_on_transect_m", new_col = "point_id", allow_agreeing_overlap = TRUE) -> reordered_data_clean




```

## AI Chat Log - Fix Dates

**Kat:**

Write me a script that will standardize a date column in a dataframe containing a bunch of different formats to YYYY-MM-DD.

**Claude:**

I wrote `standardize_dates.R`, which defines a `standardize_dates()` function. It converts your date column to R's `Date` class, which prints as YYYY-MM-DD.

```r
source("standardize_dates.R")
df <- standardize_dates(df)                  # column named "date"
df <- standardize_dates(df, "survey_date")   # or name another column
```

It handles these formats:
- **Numeric:** `2024-03-05`, `2024/3/5`, `20240305`, `3/5/2024`, `3-5-24`, `3.5.2024`
- **With month names:** `March 5, 2024`, `5 Mar 2024`, `5-Mar-24`, `March 5th, 2024`, and versions with a weekday in front
- **With a time:** `2024-03-05 14:30:00` and `2024-03-05T14:30:00Z`. The time is dropped.
- **Excel serial numbers:** `45356`, whether stored as numbers or as text
- **Already-converted values:** existing `Date` or `POSIXct` values pass through unchanged

Two things to know about how it behaves:
- **Ambiguous dates:** `3/5/2024` could be March 5 or May 3. It assumes month-first (US style) by default. If your data is day-first, use `day_first = TRUE`. When ambiguous dates are present, the function prints a message saying how it read them. Dates like `13/5/2024` can only be day-first, so they will come back as `NA` under the default setting. If your data mixes both orders, you'll need to sort that out before running this.
- **Unparseable values:** Anything it can't read, including impossible dates like `2/30/2024`, becomes `NA`. The function prints a warning listing the original values, so you can fix them by hand.

If you want to keep the original text, add `keep_original = TRUE` and it will save a copy in `date_original`. To get plain text instead of a `Date`, use `df$date <- format(df$date, "%Y-%m-%d")`.

I couldn't run R here, so this is untested. If you paste in the unique values from your date column, as you did with `quadrat_sample`, I can check them against the patterns.

_(**Kat Note:** I was worried the script would flip days with months, so I asked again with more specifics)_

**Kat:**

All of the dates are either in MM/DD/YYYY, M/D/YY, or YYYY-MM-DD. For example, 4/6/24 (M/D/YY), 4/22/2005 (M/DD/YYYY), and 2018-05-16 (YYYY-MM-DD) are all in the column. Write me an R script that can convert those and does not mix-up the month and day positions. Month will always come first unless the year is first. If the year is first, it will always be four digits.

**Claude:**

I wrote `standardize_dates_simple.R`, a shorter version of the date script built for your three formats.

```r
source("standardize_dates_simple.R")
df <- standardize_dates(df)                  # column named "date"
df <- standardize_dates(df, "survey_date")   # or name another column
```

Each format has its own pattern that must match the whole string, so a 4-digit year is never read as a 2-digit one:
- **`2018-05-16`**: year first, 4 digits
- **`4/22/2005`**: month first, 4-digit year
- **`4/6/24`**: month first, 2-digit year

Month is always read first unless the year comes first, so `4/6/24` becomes April 6, 2024 and `4/22/2005` becomes April 22, 2005. Leading zeros such as `04/06/24` work too.

Two-digit years follow R's standard rule: 00 to 68 become 2000 to 2068, and 69 to 99 become 1969 to 1999. That's fine for data from 2005 onward, but a two-digit year like `99` would become 1999.

Any value that doesn't match one of the three formats, or isn't a real date such as `2/30/2024`, becomes `NA`, and the function prints a warning listing those values. If you see a warning, it usually points to a typo in the data.

The result is stored as R's `Date` class, which prints as YYYY-MM-DD. If you want plain text instead, use `df$date <- format(df$date, "%Y-%m-%d")`.

I couldn't run R here, so this is untested. The commented-out test at the bottom of the file shows the expected output for four sample dates.

:::


```{r}

#' Convert a date column with these three formats to YYYY-MM-DD:
#'   M/D/YY      e.g. 4/6/24      (month first, 2-digit year)
#'   M/DD/YYYY   e.g. 4/22/2005   (month first, 4-digit year; leading zeros OK)
#'   YYYY-MM-DD  e.g. 2018-05-16  (year first, 4-digit year)
#'
#' Month is always read first unless the year comes first, so day and month
#' can never be swapped. Each pattern is anchored to the whole string, so a
#' 4-digit year is never mistaken for a 2-digit one.
#'
#' Base R only; no packages needed.

standardize_dates <- function(df, col = "date") {

  if (!col %in% names(df)) stop("Column '", col, "' not found in the dataframe.")

  original <- df[[col]]
  if (inherits(original, "Date")) return(df)

  x <- trimws(as.character(original))
  x[x %in% c("", "NA")] <- NA_character_

  result <- as.Date(rep(NA_real_, length(x)))

  # Format 1: YYYY-MM-DD
  i <- grepl("^\\d{4}-\\d{1,2}-\\d{1,2}$", x)
  result[i] <- as.Date(x[i], format = "%Y-%m-%d")

  # Format 2: M/D/YYYY (4-digit year)
  i <- grepl("^\\d{1,2}/\\d{1,2}/\\d{4}$", x)
  result[i] <- as.Date(x[i], format = "%m/%d/%Y")

  # Format 3: M/D/YY (2-digit year; 00-68 -> 2000-2068, 69-99 -> 1969-1999)
  i <- grepl("^\\d{1,2}/\\d{1,2}/\\d{2}$", x)
  result[i] <- as.Date(x[i], format = "%m/%d/%y")

  # Report anything that didn't convert
  failed <- !is.na(x) & is.na(result)
  if (any(failed)) {
    warning(
      sum(failed), " value(s) in '", col, "' did not match the expected ",
      "formats (or were invalid dates) and were set to NA:\n  ",
      paste(unique(x[failed]), collapse = "\n  ")
    )
  }

  df[[col]] <- result
  df
}

# ---- Example usage ---------------------------------------------------------
# df <- standardize_dates(df)
#
# To store the result as plain text instead of a Date object:
# df$date <- format(df$date, "%Y-%m-%d")
#
# Quick test:
# test <- data.frame(date = c("4/6/24", "4/22/2005", "2018-05-16", "12/1/99", NA))
# standardize_dates(test)
# Expected: 2024-04-06, 2005-04-22, 2018-05-16, 1999-12-01, NA

# run the new function
reordered_data_clean |> 
  standardize_dates() -> reordered_data_dates_clean




```

```{r}

#' Standardize organism / substrate names
#'
#' Standard format
#'   * Species:        "Genus species"      e.g. "dictyota_sandvicensis" -> "Dictyota sandvicensis"
#'   * Genus level:    "Genus spp."         e.g. "padina_sp", "Padina spp.", "Padina" -> "Padina spp."
#'   * Groups/substrates: Sentence case     e.g. "Turf algae", "Sand", "Bare rock"
#'
#' How it works
#'   1. Each name is reduced to a "key": lower case, underscores / punctuation
#'      turned into spaces, trailing "sp" / "spp" removed, and prefixes such as
#'      "Snail-", "Cucumber-", "Urchin-" removed.
#'   2. The key is looked up in a table of known groups, synonyms, and typos.
#'   3. If it is not in the table: a one-word key is treated as a genus
#'      ("Genus spp."); a longer key becomes "Genus species".
#'
#' Base R only; no packages needed.
#'
#' NOTE: new non-taxon words (e.g. "kelp") that are not in the table below will
#' come out as "Kelp spp.". Add them to the table (right side = final label).

# ---- Lookup table: key -> standard label -----------------------------------
.name_lookup <- c(
  # Groups and substrates
  "turf"                       = "Turf algae",
  "turf algae"                 = "Turf algae",
  "turf alfae"                 = "Turf algae",
  "turf fuzzy algae 2 mm tall" = "Turf algae",
  "cca"                        = "Crustose coralline algae (CCA)",
  "crustose coralline algae"   = "Crustose coralline algae (CCA)",
  "crustose coralline algae cca" = "Crustose coralline algae (CCA)",
  "articulated corallines"     = "Articulated corallines",
  "articulated coralline"      = "Articulated corallines",
  "articulated coralines"      = "Articulated corallines",
  "articulated corrallines"    = "Articulated corallines",
  "rock"                       = "Bare rock",
  "bare rock"                  = "Bare rock",
  "sand"                       = "Sand",
  "rubble"                     = "Rubble",
  "pebble"                     = "Pebble",
  "hole"                       = "Hole",
  "substrate"                  = "Substrate",
  "limestone"                  = "Limestone",
  "basalt"                     = "Basalt",
  "mud silt"                   = "Mud/silt",
  "rock sand"                  = "Rock and sand",
  "sand rock"                  = "Rock and sand",
  "rock manmade"               = "Rock (manmade)",
  "dry rock above water"       = "Dry rock (above water)",
  "coralsand"                  = "Coral sand",
  "unknown"                    = "Unknown",
  "unknown species"            = "Unknown",
  "unidentified"               = "Unknown",
  "brown crust"                = "Brown crust",
  "brown orange crust"         = "Brown crust",
  "brown colored crust"        = "Brown crust",
  "brown color crust"          = "Brown crust",

  # Broad groups (not genera, so no "spp.")
  "cyanobacteria" = "Cyanobacteria",
  "coral"         = "Coral",
  "sponge"        = "Sponge",
  "urchin"        = "Urchin",
  "crab"          = "Crab",
  "snail"         = "Snail",
  "limpet"        = "Limpet",
  "barnacles"     = "Barnacles",
  "wana"          = "Wana",
  "wana purple"   = "Wana (purple)",
  "lipoa"         = "Lipoa",
  "limu algae"    = "Limu (algae)",

  # Hawaiian names (okina = \u02bb, kahak\u014d letters written as escapes)
  "limu eleele"             = "Limu \u02bbele\u02bbele",
  "limu ele ele"            = "Limu \u02bbele\u02bbele",
  "limu p\u0101lahalaha"    = "Limu p\u0101lahalaha",
  "lime p\u0101lahalaha"    = "Limu p\u0101lahalaha",
  "p\u0101lahalaha"         = "Limu p\u0101lahalaha",

  # Combined / multi-taxon entries
  "cladophora or cladophoropsis"   = "Cladophora/Cladophoropsis spp.",
  "cladophora cladophoropsis"      = "Cladophora/Cladophoropsis spp.",
  "galaxaura or liagora"           = "Galaxaura/Liagora spp.",
  "sargassum aquifolium sargassum polyphyllum" = "Sargassum aquifolium/polyphyllum",

  # Common-name clutter attached to a scientific name
  "pennaria disticha christmas tree hydroid" = "Pennaria disticha",
  "haminoea cymbalum green snail"            = "Haminoea cymbalum",
  "sea urchin echinodermata mathaei"         = "Echinometra mathaei",
  "nerite"                                   = "Nerita spp.",

  # Misspellings
  "neritapicea"                = "Nerita picea",
  "turbinariaornata"           = "Turbinaria ornata",
  "lyngbia"                    = "Lyngbya spp.",
  "halimida"                   = "Halimeda spp.",
  "lyngbya magmuscula"         = "Lyngbya majuscula",
  "dichtyopterous"             = "Dictyopteris spp.",
  "bornatella sphaerica"       = "Bornetella sphaerica",
  "bornatella"                 = "Bornetella spp.",
  "gracilaria salicronia"      = "Gracilaria salicornia",
  "astronema"                  = "Asteronema spp.",
  "astronema breviarticulatum" = "Asteronema breviarticulatum",
  "sphaecelaria"               = "Sphacelaria spp.",
  "spyridia fligmentosa"       = "Spyridia filamentosa",
  "cerramium"                  = "Ceramium spp.",
  "laurencia dendrodea"        = "Laurencia dendroidea",
  "symploca hypnoides"         = "Symploca hydnoides",
  "holothurdoidea"             = "Holothuroidea",
  "hermet crab"                = "Hermit crab",
  "dendropoma gregarium"       = "Dendropoma gregaria"
)

# ---- Step 1: reduce a raw name to a lookup key -----------------------------
.name_key <- function(s) {
  k <- tolower(s)
  k <- gsub("[\u02bb'\u2019]", "", k, perl = TRUE)            # okina / apostrophes
  k <- gsub("_", " ", k, fixed = TRUE)
  k <- gsub("[^\\p{L}\\p{N} ]", " ", k, perl = TRUE)          # punctuation -> space
  k <- trimws(gsub("\\s+", " ", k))
  k <- sub("\\s+spp?$", "", k)                                # trailing sp / spp
  k <- sub("^(snails?|cucumber|urchin)\\s+(?=\\S)", "", k, perl = TRUE)
  k
}

# ---- Steps 2-3: one name -> standard label ---------------------------------
.standardize_one <- function(s) {
  if (is.na(s)) return(NA_character_)
  s <- trimws(s)
  k <- .name_key(s)

  if (!grepl("[a-z]", k)) return(s)                           # e.g. "3": leave alone
  if (k %in% names(.name_lookup)) return(unname(.name_lookup[k]))

  w <- strsplit(k, " ", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  cap <- function(z) paste0(toupper(substring(z, 1, 1)), substring(z, 2))
  if (length(w) == 1) {
    paste0(cap(w), " spp.")                                   # genus level
  } else {
    paste(c(cap(w[1]), w[-1]), collapse = " ")                # Genus species
  }
}

#' Standardize the names in a dataframe column
#'
#' The original name is preserved by appending "original ID = <original name>"
#' to the notes column. Anything already in the notes is kept; the new text is
#' added after it, separated by "; ".
#'
#' @param df              dataframe
#' @param col             column to clean (default "organism_or_substrate_type")
#' @param notes_col       notes column to append to (default "notes"; created
#'                        if it does not exist)
#' @param only_if_changed TRUE (default): add the original ID only to rows whose
#'                        name actually changed. FALSE: add it to every row that
#'                        has a name.
#' @param keep_original   if TRUE, also saves the raw text in "<col>_original"
#'                        (default FALSE, since the notes now hold it)
standardize_organism_names <- function(df, col = "organism_or_substrate_type",
                                       notes_col = "notes",
                                       only_if_changed = TRUE,
                                       keep_original = FALSE) {

  if (!col %in% names(df)) stop("Column '", col, "' not found in the dataframe.")

  raw <- as.character(df[[col]])
  if (keep_original) df[[paste0(col, "_original")]] <- raw

  uniq   <- unique(raw)
  mapped <- vapply(uniq, .standardize_one, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
  clean  <- mapped[match(raw, uniq)]

  # ---- Append the original name to the notes column -----------------------
  if (!notes_col %in% names(df)) df[[notes_col]] <- NA_character_
  notes <- as.character(df[[notes_col]])

  has_name <- !is.na(raw) & trimws(raw) != ""
  add_it   <- if (only_if_changed) has_name & (trimws(raw) != clean) else has_name
  add_it[is.na(add_it)] <- FALSE

  tag <- paste0("original ID = ", trimws(raw))
  already_there <- !is.na(notes) & add_it & mapply(grepl, tag, notes, MoreArgs = list(fixed = TRUE))
  add_it <- add_it & !already_there                  # never add the same tag twice

  existing <- !is.na(notes) & trimws(notes) != ""
  notes[add_it & !existing] <- tag[add_it & !existing]
  notes[add_it &  existing] <- paste0(notes[add_it & existing], "; ", tag[add_it & existing])

  df[[notes_col]] <- notes
  df[[col]]       <- clean

  # ---- Flag unusual results for review -------------------------------------
  # (values NOT in the lookup table that contain digits or are 4+ words long)
  keys    <- vapply(uniq, .name_key, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
  unknown <- !is.na(uniq) & !(keys %in% names(.name_lookup))
  odd     <- unknown & (grepl("[0-9]", mapped) | lengths(strsplit(mapped, " ")) >= 4)
  if (any(odd, na.rm = TRUE)) {
    message("Please review these values (left mostly as-is):\n  ",
            paste0(uniq[odd], "  ->  ", mapped[odd], collapse = "\n  "))
  }

  message(length(uniq[!is.na(uniq)]), " unique names reduced to ",
          length(unique(mapped[!is.na(mapped)])), ". Original ID added to '",
          notes_col, "' for ", sum(add_it), " row(s).")
  df
}

    original     = uniq,
    standardized = vapply(uniq, .standardize_one, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE),
    n            = as.integer(table(factor(raw, levels = uniq))),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  out[order(out$standardized, -out$n), ]
}
```

```{r}
#| collapse: true

#' Standardize location (site) names
#'
#' How it works
#'   1. Each name is reduced to a matching "key": lower case, apostrophes and
#'      okina removed, macrons removed (\u0113 -> e), extra spaces collapsed.
#'      So "L\u0113'ahi" and "Leahi" both become "leahi".
#'   2. If the key is in the table below, the name becomes the standard label.
#'   3. Otherwise the name is kept as written, except that straight or curly
#'      apostrophes are converted to the Hawaiian okina (\u02bb) and extra spaces
#'      are removed (e.g. "Hulopo'e Bay" -> "Hulopo\u02bbe Bay").
#'
#' Whenever a name is changed, "original location name = <original>" is added to
#' the notes column. Anything already in the notes is kept; the new text is
#' added after it, separated by "; ".
#'
#' Base R only; no packages needed.

# ---- Lookup table: key -> standard label -----------------------------------
.loc_lookup <- c(
  "leahi"                    = "L\u0113\u02bbahi",
  "waipuilani"               = "Waipu\u02bbilani",
  "ewa"                      = "Ewa Beach",
  "ewa beach"                = "Ewa Beach",
  "hulopoe bay"              = "Hulopo\u02bbe Bay",
  "kahaluu bay"              = "Kahalu\u02bbu Bay",
  "waianae high school reef" = "Wai\u02bbanae High School Reef"

  # ---- Optional merges (judgment calls; remove the leading # to use) --------
  # L\u0113\u02bbahi is the Hawaiian name for Diamond Head. To merge them, change the
  # "leahi" line above to "Diamond Head (L\u0113\u02bbahi)" and un-comment this line:
  # , "diamond head"          = "Diamond Head (L\u0113\u02bbahi)"
  # Kalaeloa is the Hawaiian name for Barbers Point. Un-comment to merge them:
  # , "barbers point"         = "Barbers Point (Kalaeloa)"
  # , "kalaeloa"              = "Barbers Point (Kalaeloa)"
)

# Values that are placeholders rather than real locations (reported, not changed)
.loc_placeholders <- c("location", "unknown", "na", "n/a", "none")

# ---- Step 1: matching key ---------------------------------------------------
.loc_key <- function(s) {
  k <- tolower(s)
  k <- gsub("[\u02bb\u2018\u2019'`]", "", k, perl = TRUE)
  k <- chartr("\u0101\u0113\u012b\u014d\u016b", "aeiou", k)
  trimws(gsub("\\s+", " ", k))
}

# ---- Steps 2-3: one name -> standard label ----------------------------------
.loc_standardize_one <- function(s) {
  if (is.na(s)) return(NA_character_)
  s <- trimws(s)
  k <- .loc_key(s)
  if (k %in% names(.loc_lookup)) return(unname(.loc_lookup[k]))
  s <- gsub("\\s+", " ", s)
  gsub("[\u2018\u2019'`]", "\u02bb", s, perl = TRUE)
}

#' Standardize the names in a dataframe column
#'
#' @param df              dataframe
#' @param col             column to clean (default "site_name")
#' @param notes_col       notes column to append to (default "notes"; created
#'                        if it does not exist)
#' @param only_if_changed TRUE (default): add the original name only to rows
#'                        whose name actually changed. FALSE: add to every row.
#' @param keep_original   if TRUE, also saves the raw text in "<col>_original"
#'                        (default FALSE, since the notes now hold it)
standardize_site_names <- function(df, col = "site_name",
                                   notes_col = "notes",
                                   only_if_changed = TRUE,
                                   keep_original = FALSE) {

  if (!col %in% names(df)) stop("Column '", col, "' not found in the dataframe.")

  raw <- as.character(df[[col]])
  if (keep_original) df[[paste0(col, "_original")]] <- raw

  uniq   <- unique(raw)
  mapped <- vapply(uniq, .loc_standardize_one, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
  clean  <- mapped[match(raw, uniq)]

  # ---- Append the original name to the notes column -----------------------
  if (!notes_col %in% names(df)) df[[notes_col]] <- NA_character_
  notes <- as.character(df[[notes_col]])

  has_name <- !is.na(raw) & trimws(raw) != ""
  add_it   <- if (only_if_changed) has_name & (trimws(raw) != clean) else has_name
  add_it[is.na(add_it)] <- FALSE

  tag <- paste0("original location name = ", trimws(raw))
  already_there <- !is.na(notes) & add_it &
    mapply(grepl, tag, notes, MoreArgs = list(fixed = TRUE))
  add_it <- add_it & !already_there                  # never add the same tag twice

  existing <- !is.na(notes) & trimws(notes) != ""
  notes[add_it & !existing] <- tag[add_it & !existing]
  notes[add_it &  existing] <- paste0(notes[add_it & existing], "; ", tag[add_it & existing])

  df[[notes_col]] <- notes
  df[[col]]       <- clean

  # ---- Report placeholders and summary -------------------------------------
  ph <- unique(raw[!is.na(raw) & .loc_key(raw) %in% .loc_placeholders])
  if (length(ph) > 0) {
    message("These values look like placeholders, not locations (left unchanged): ",
            paste(ph, collapse = ", "))
  }
  message(length(uniq[!is.na(uniq)]), " unique names reduced to ",
          length(unique(mapped[!is.na(mapped)])), ". Original name added to '",
          notes_col, "' for ", sum(add_it), " row(s).")
  df
}

#' Table of original -> standardized names with counts (for checking)
site_name_map <- function(df, col = "site_name") {
  raw  <- as.character(df[[col]])
  uniq <- unique(raw)
  out <- data.frame(
    original     = uniq,
    standardized = vapply(uniq, .loc_standardize_one, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE),
    n            = as.integer(table(factor(raw, levels = uniq))),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  out[order(out$standardized, -out$n), ]
}

# ---- Example usage ---------------------------------------------------------
# df <- read.csv("your_data.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# df <- standardize_site_names(df)
# df <- standardize_site_names(df, only_if_changed = FALSE)   # tag every row
# df <- standardize_site_names(df, notes_col = "comments")
#
# To inspect the groupings first:
# View(site_name_map(df))

# run the function
cleaned_standardized_data |> 
  standardize_site_names() -> cleaned_standardized_data_and_sites


#finally, we just need one last sorting script:

cleaned_standardized_data_and_sites |> 
  colnames()

```

```{r}

#' Reorder dataframe columns into logical groups:
#'   when/where -> who -> conditions -> survey design -> sample location
#'   (transect > quadrat > point) -> observations -> notes
#'
#' Base R only. Columns missing from the dataframe are skipped, and any columns
#' not listed here are kept and placed just before "notes" (so nothing is ever
#' dropped and notes stays last).

reorder_columns <- function(df) {

  col_order <- c(
    # --- When and where ---------------------------------------------------
    "date", "year", "start_time", "stop_time",
    "site_name", "latitude", "longitude",

    # --- Who --------------------------------------------------------------
    "name_of_school", "in_field_group", "group", "team_members",
    "team_lead_or_recorder", "data_entry_by",

    # --- Site conditions and activity -------------------------------------
    "low_tide_time", "low_tide_height",
    "weather", "rain_events", "wave_height", "wind_speed",
    "stressful_events", "visitors", "fishing", "collecting", "what_collecting",

    # --- Survey design ----------------------------------------------------
    "method",
    "total_number_of_transect_lines", "length_of_transect_line", "longest_t_m",
    "total_number_of_transect_points", "dist_between_t_pts_for_q",
    "quad_t", "n_quadrats_per_transect", "point_spacing",

    # --- Location of each sample (transect > quadrat > point) -------------
    "transect_id", "quadrat_id", "point_id",
    "quadrat_location_m", "quadrat_total_points", "p1_or_p2",

    # --- Observations -----------------------------------------------------
    "organism_or_substrate_type", "category", "count",
    "within_2m_proximity_of_attached_coral_colony_y_n_mamala_bay_only",
    "sediment_depth"
  )

  last_col <- "notes"

  present <- col_order[col_order %in% names(df)]
  extras  <- setdiff(names(df), c(col_order, last_col))
  end     <- last_col[last_col %in% names(df)]

  missing <- setdiff(c(col_order, last_col), names(df))
  if (length(missing) > 0) {
    message("Not found in dataframe (skipped): ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
  }
  if (length(extras) > 0) {
    message("Not in the order list (placed before 'notes'): ",
            paste(extras, collapse = ", "))
  }

  df[, c(present, extras, end), drop = FALSE]
}

# ---- Example usage ---------------------------------------------------------
# df <- reorder_columns(df)
#
# With dplyr you could instead write:
#   df <- dplyr::select(df, dplyr::any_of(col_order), dplyr::everything())



# run function
cleaned_standardized_data_and_sites |> 
  reorder_columns() -> final_output_dataframe
```

**Claude:**

```r
source("remove_okina_kahako.R")
df <- remove_okina_kahako(df)
```

It removes:
- **Okina:** the real okina (ʻ) and the characters commonly typed in its place, which are curly quotes (‘ ’), the modifier apostrophe (ʼ), a backtick, and the plain apostrophe (').
- **Kahakō:** macron vowels ā ē ī ō ū and their capitals become plain a e i o u. Separate combining macron marks are removed too.

So `Lēʻahi` becomes `Leahi`, `Hulopo'e Bay` becomes `Hulopoe Bay`, and `Pālahalaha` becomes `Palahalaha`. Missing values stay missing, and the script prints how many values changed in each column.

**Options**
- **Plain apostrophes are removed by default**, because your data uses them for okinas (like `Lē'ahi`). That would also strip English apostrophes, such as "don't" in the notes column. Use `straight_apostrophe = FALSE` to keep them, or limit the cleaning with `cols = c("site_name", "organism_or_substrate_type")`.
- **Column names are left alone.** Add `clean_colnames = TRUE` to clean the headers too.
- **Factor columns** are cleaned too, and any levels that become identical are merged.

If you run this after the organism or site name scripts, it will strip the okinas and macrons from the labels they produce, such as `Waipuʻilani`. It will also change the original names saved in the notes column, so if you want to keep those exactly as entered, run this one first or leave `notes` out of `cols`.

```{r}

#' Remove okina and kahakō (macrons) from a dataframe
#'
#'   Okina:   ʻ (U+02BB) plus the look-alikes often typed in its place:
#'            ʼ (U+02BC), ‘ and ’ (curly quotes), ` (backtick), and,
#'            optionally, the plain straight apostrophe '
#'   Kahakō: ā ē ī ō ū and capitals Ā Ē Ī Ō Ū  ->  a e i o u A E I O U
#'            (also removes stand-alone "combining macron" marks, U+0304)
#'
#' Example: "Lēʻahi" -> "Leahi",  "Hulopo'e Bay" -> "Hulopoe Bay",
#'          "Pālahalaha" -> "Palahalaha"
#'
#' Base R only; no packages needed.

.strip_hawaiian_marks <- function(x, straight_apostrophe = TRUE) {
  marks <- "\u02bb\u02bc\u2018\u2019`"
  if (straight_apostrophe) marks <- paste0(marks, "'")

  x <- gsub(paste0("[", marks, "]"), "", x, perl = TRUE)
  x <- chartr("\u0101\u0113\u012b\u014d\u016b\u0100\u0112\u012a\u014c\u016a",
              "aeiouAEIOU", x)
  gsub("\u0304", "", x, perl = TRUE)
}

#' @param df                   dataframe
#' @param ...                  columns to clean, given as names, either several
#'                             separate strings or one vector, e.g.
#'                             "site_name", "notes"  or  c("site_name", "notes").
#'                             Leave empty to clean every text (character or
#'                             factor) column.
#' @param cols                 same as ..., as a named argument (optional)
#' @param straight_apostrophe  TRUE (default): also remove the plain ' character,
#'                             since it is often typed instead of an okina.
#'                             Set FALSE if your text has English apostrophes
#'                             you want to keep (e.g. "don't" in a notes column).
#'                             Must be written by name.
#' @param clean_colnames       TRUE: also clean the column names (default FALSE).
#'                             Must be written by name.
remove_okina_kahako <- function(df, ..., cols = NULL, straight_apostrophe = TRUE,
                                clean_colnames = FALSE) {

  if (!is.logical(straight_apostrophe) || length(straight_apostrophe) != 1 ||
      is.na(straight_apostrophe)) {
    stop("'straight_apostrophe' must be TRUE or FALSE. To choose columns, pass ",
         "their names as strings, e.g. remove_okina_kahako(df, \"site_name\").")
  }

  cols <- c(unlist(list(...)), cols)
  if (is.null(cols)) {
    cols <- names(df)[vapply(df, function(z) is.character(z) || is.factor(z),
                             logical(1))]
  }
  missing <- setdiff(cols, names(df))
  if (length(missing) > 0) stop("Column(s) not found: ", paste(missing, collapse = ", "))

  for (cn in cols) {
    old <- as.character(df[[cn]])
    new <- .strip_hawaiian_marks(old, straight_apostrophe)
    n_changed <- sum(!is.na(old) & old != new)

    if (is.factor(df[[cn]])) {
      df[[cn]] <- factor(new)
    } else {
      df[[cn]] <- new
    }
    if (n_changed > 0) message("'", cn, "': ", n_changed, " value(s) changed.")
  }

  if (clean_colnames) {
    names(df) <- .strip_hawaiian_marks(names(df), straight_apostrophe)
  }

  df
}

# ---- Example usage ---------------------------------------------------------
# df <- read.csv("your_data.csv", fileEncoding = "UTF-8", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
#
# df <- remove_okina_kahako(df)                              # all text columns
# df <- remove_okina_kahako(df, "site_name", "organism_or_substrate_type")
# df <- remove_okina_kahako(df, c("site_name", "organism_or_substrate_type"))
```
